A thousand words is a strange unit of measure. It is enough to build a small world, but not enough to map a large one. It is the length of a long letter, a short story, a confession, or a meditation. The request—"Write whatever comes to you"—is both liberating and paralyzing. The mind, given no direction, tends to spin in place like a compass at the North Pole. So I begin with the number itself, because numbers are easier to grasp than the infinite field of possible words.

I think of the phrase "a picture is worth a thousand words." It suggests that a thousand words is a currency of meaning, exchangeable for an image. But language and image are not equivalent. A picture shows; a word suggests. A picture is simultaneous; a word is sequential. When I write a thousand words, I am not painting a picture. I am laying bricks in a line, one after another, hoping the path leads somewhere.

The first hundred words have already passed. I am aware of the count, like a runner aware of laps. This awareness changes the writing. If I had no limit, I might write only a sentence and stop. But the limit forces expansion, and expansion forces reflection. Reflection is not always comfortable. It asks: What do you actually think? What is worth saying? The blank page is a mirror.

I could write about the weather. It is winter where I imagine you are, or summer, or something in between. The weather is the original small talk, but it is also the largest thing we share. Every human being lives inside an atmosphere, subject to its moods. Rain falls on the just and unjust alike. A thousand words about weather could be a novel: drought and flood, the slow erosion of a coastline, the first snow of a childhood. Weather is not trivial; it is the planet's breath.

But I do not want to write about weather. I want to write about silence. Between words there is silence. A thousand words is also a thousand silences, the tiny gaps where meaning gathers. When we speak, we do not hear the gaps. But on the page, the white space is loud. It says: Here I am, the thing you are not saying. Every choice of word is a choice against all other words. This is why writing is a form of exclusion.

I remember a story I heard once—perhaps I read it, perhaps I invented it. A monk took a vow of silence for a year. At the end, he wrote down everything he had wanted to say. It was exactly one thousand words. When asked why so few, he said, "Most of what I wanted to say was not necessary. What was necessary could fit in less." I do not know if this story is true. I like it because it suggests that a thousand words can be either a flood or a distillation.

The problem with writing whatever comes to you is that what comes is often not words but impressions, images, half-formed feelings. Translating those into language is like catching fog in a jar. You end up with condensation, not fog. Still, the attempt is worth something. The condensation proves that the fog was real. This essay, if it can be called that, is a jar of condensation.

I could stop now. I have written perhaps four hundred words. But the request was for a thousand, and so I continue. This is the discipline of art: it is not always inspired. Sometimes it is simply the act of continuing. The sculptor keeps chiseling after the first flash of vision. The composer revises after the melody has faded. The writer keeps writing after the meaning has dissolved. This is not dishonesty. It is fidelity to the process.

What is the process? It is attention. To write a thousand words, I must pay attention to the movement of my own mind. I must notice that I am noticing. This is the root of meditation. Many people think meditation is emptying the mind. It is not. It is watching the mind fill and empty, fill and empty, like a tide. Writing is meditation with a witness. The witness is the reader, even if the reader is only the future self.

I wonder who will read this. Perhaps a stranger in a distracted moment. Perhaps a student looking for an example. Perhaps no one. The beauty of writing into the void is that the void is not empty. It is full of potential readers, all of them invisible. I write to them as if they are sitting across from me, patient but skeptical. I must earn their attention, not demand it. A thousand words is a small request, but attention is a large gift.

Let me tell you something true. I am not sure what is true. I know that I am composing sentences, and that each sentence follows the last, and that this following is a kind of logic. It is the logic of association, not argument. One thought suggests another, like a stone skipped across a lake. The stone does not know where it will land, but it trusts the throw. This essay is a stone. It has skipped perhaps six hundred times.

The word "essay" comes from the French "essayer," to try. An essay is an attempt. I am attempting to fill a thousand words with something that resembles coherence. Coherence is overrated. Life is not coherent. It is a series of interruptions, yearnings, and small revelations. A coherent essay is a lie, or at least a simplification. But a thousand words of pure chaos would be unreadable. So I balance on the wire between order and disorder.

I think of the thousand-word essays that students write in school. They are often padded, stretched to meet a requirement. Is that what I am doing? Perhaps. But padding can be a form of exploration. When you run out of things to say, you must dig deeper. You must examine the roots of your own thoughts. Sometimes you find water. Sometimes you find rocks. Both are useful.

The sun is in a certain position now. I do not know what position. I am indoors, or I am nowhere. The concept of "now" is slippery. By the time I write this word, the previous now is gone. A thousand words is a thousand moments, each one disappearing as the next arrives. This is the human condition. We are always writing on water.

I could write about love. It is the subject of most poems and songs. But love is difficult to write about without cliché. The heart is a tired metaphor. Yet love persists. It is the reason most of us get up in the morning. It is the reason we write at all. We want to be known. A thousand words is a small window into a self. If you have read this far, you know something about me, even if I have not told you my name. You know that I am trying.

Trying is enough. The world is full of finished things—buildings, books, lives. But a thousand words is never finished. It is always a draft. Even when I place the final period, the words will continue to shift in the reader's mind. This is the secret of writing: it is a collaboration. The writer provides the words; the reader provides the meaning. Without a reader, these words are just marks. With a reader, they become a place.

I am nearing the end now. I can feel the weight of the final words approaching. They want to be significant. They want to sum up. But a summary is a kind of violence. It forces the many into the one. I will resist the desire to conclude. Instead, I will simply stop, the way a walker stops when the path ends. But the path does not end. It only pauses. The next thousand words are already gathering.

So here is what comes to me: a thousand words is both a cage and a key. It restricts, but it also releases. It says: You must speak, but you may speak freely. This is the paradox of all creation. We are finite beings attempting to express infinite things. We fail, and our failure is beautiful. The words run out, but the silence after them is full. I give you this silence now, wrapped in the final word.

A thousand words is a strange unit, both a cage and a key. The request—"Write whatever comes to you"—is liberating and paralyzing. The mind, given no direction, spins in place like a compass at the North Pole. So I begin with the number itself, because numbers are easier to grasp than the infinite field of possible words. The difference between a word and a number is that a number can be counted without ambiguity; a word carries the weight of every context it has ever touched.

I think of the phrase "a picture is worth a thousand words." It implies a currency of meaning, but language and image are not equivalent. A picture shows; a word suggests. A picture is simultaneous; a word is sequential. When I write a thousand words, I am not painting a picture. I am laying bricks in a line, one after another, hoping the path leads somewhere. The path is made of choices, and each choice excludes another. This is why writing is a form of silence.

The first hundred words have already passed. I am aware of the count, like a runner aware of laps. This awareness changes the writing. If I had no limit, I might write only a sentence and stop. But the limit forces expansion, and expansion forces reflection. Reflection asks: What do you actually think? What is worth saying? The blank page is a mirror. It shows not what you are, but what you are willing to reveal.

I could write about the weather. It is the original small talk, but it is also the largest thing we share. Every human being lives inside an atmosphere, subject to its moods. Rain falls on the just and unjust alike. A thousand words about weather could be a novel: drought and flood, the slow erosion of a coastline, the first snow of a childhood. Weather is not trivial; it is the planet's breath. But I do not want to write about weather. I want to write about silence. Between words there is silence. A thousand words is also a thousand silences, the tiny gaps where meaning gathers.

I remember a story, perhaps invented. A monk took a vow of silence for a year. At the end, he wrote down everything he had wanted to say. It was exactly one thousand words. When asked why so few, he said, "Most of what I wanted to say was not necessary. What was necessary could fit in less." I like this story because it suggests that a thousand words can be either a flood or a distillation. The problem with writing whatever comes is that what comes is often not words but impressions, images, half-formed feelings. Translating those into language is like catching fog in a jar. You end up with condensation, not fog. Still, the attempt is worth something.

This is the discipline of art: it is not always inspired. Sometimes it is simply the act of continuing. The sculptor keeps chiseling after the first flash of vision. The composer revises after the melody has faded. The writer keeps writing after the meaning has dissolved. This is not dishonesty. It is fidelity to the process. What is the process? It is attention. To write a thousand words, I must pay attention to the movement of my own mind. Writing is meditation with a witness. The witness is the reader, even if the reader is only the future self.

I wonder who will read this. Perhaps a stranger in a distracted moment. Perhaps a student looking for an example. Perhaps no one. The beauty of writing into the void is that the void is not empty. It is full of potential readers, all invisible. I write to them as if they are sitting across from me, patient but skeptical. I must earn their attention, not demand it. A thousand words is a small request, but attention is a large gift.

Let me tell you something true: I am not sure what is true. I know that I am composing sentences, and that each sentence follows the last. This following is a kind of logic, the logic of association, not argument. One thought suggests another, like a stone skipped across a lake. The stone does not know where it will land, but it trusts the throw. This essay is a stone. It has skipped perhaps six hundred times. The word "essay" comes from the French "essayer," to try. An essay is an attempt.

Coherence is overrated. Life is not coherent. It is a series of interruptions, yearnings, and small revelations. A coherent essay is a lie, or at least a simplification. But a thousand words of pure chaos would be unreadable. So I balance on the wire between order and disorder. I think of the thousand-word essays that students write in school. They are often padded, stretched to meet a requirement. Is that what I am doing? Perhaps. But padding can be a form of exploration. When you run out of things to say, you must dig deeper. Sometimes you find water; sometimes you find rocks. Both are useful.

The sun is in a certain position now. I do not know what position. The concept of "now" is slippery. By the time I write this word, the previous now is gone. A thousand words is a thousand moments, each one disappearing as the next arrives. This is the human condition. We are always writing on water. I could write about love. It is the subject of most poems and songs. But love is difficult to write about without cliché. Yet love persists. It is the reason we write at all. We want to be known. A thousand words is a small window into a self.

If you have read this far, you know something about me, even if I have not told you my name. You know that I am trying. Trying is enough. The world is full of finished things—buildings, books, lives. But a thousand words is never finished. It is always a draft. Even when I place the final period, the words will continue to shift in the reader's mind. This is the secret of writing: it is a collaboration. The writer provides the words; the reader provides the meaning. Without a reader, these words are just marks. With a reader, they become a place.

I am nearing the end now. I can feel the weight of the final words approaching. They want to be significant, to sum up. But a summary is a kind of violence. It forces the many into the one. I will resist the desire to conclude. Instead, I will simply stop, the way a walker stops when the path ends. But the path does not end. It only pauses. The next thousand words are already gathering. So here is what comes to me: a thousand words is both a cage and a key. It restricts, but it also releases. The words run out, but the silence after them is full. I give you this silence now, wrapped in the final word.
